tagline: Tannery roads and mountain resorts behind a Catskill clove drive
intro: Mountain Cloves links 41 miles of roads in the northern high peaks of the Catskills. Route 23A passes Hunter Mountain before descending through Kaaterskill Clove toward the Hudson Valley. New York State approved the branched scenic byway in 2013. The state transportation department identifies scenic, recreational, historic and natural themes, linking its mountain and valley views with the Hudson River School painters. A separate branch, Route 214, narrows the landscape to Stony Clove Notch between Hunter and Plateau mountains.

One branch began with hemlock bark: Colonel William Edwards built the predecessor of Route 214 to supply his Hunter tannery. Open by 1849, it became the Stoney Clove Turnpike in 1873, serving hotels and resorts. The numbered highway came in 1930; between 1946 and 1956, Lanesville residents fought to rebuild an unsafe school-bus route. In 1994, the town of Hunter, the Catskill Center for Conservation and Development and Greene County planners nominated roads through Stony, Kaaterskill and Platte cloves for the state scenic-roads program.

For the eastward drive, Route 23A becomes Hunter village’s main street, then meets Route 214 at Stony Clove Notch. Past the junction, Plateau, Sugarloaf, Twin and Indian Head mountains rise south of the road before Tannersville. Continue through Haines Falls and descend into Kaaterskill Clove; the road levels just west of Palenville.

moments.title: Tannersville
moments.text: Pastel buildings and cartoon-like shutter paintings give Tannersville’s downtown its unusual palette. The Hunter Foundation’s Paint Program grew from local artist Elena Patterson’s vision, supported by Mayor Glenn Weyant, sponsors and residents. The village began with lumber mills and tanneries; after tanning collapsed in the mid-19th century, summer resorts gradually took its place. Rail service arrived in 1882, but the automobile later loosened visitors’ ties to a single summer destination. Route 23A is the village’s Main Street. The village sits just west of the high ground dividing drainage toward the Schoharie from water descending east through Kaaterskill Clove to the Hudson Valley.
moments.notice: Downtown buildings wear multicolored pastels, with cartoon-like pictures on some shutters.

moments.title: Kaaterskill Falls
moments.text: Kaaterskill Falls drops in two stages between Haines Falls and Palenville. The shelf between the cascades marks a boundary between Devonian rock formations, with a large pool between the falls. Thomas Cole first visited in 1825, and the falls became a subject for Hudson River School painters. Asher Durand’s Kindred Spirits combines the falls and neighboring clove features into an imagined view. The landscape in that painting is a composition, rather than a single viewpoint to seek out. Cole’s paintings helped attract affluent visitors to the Catskill Mountain House and neighboring hotels; the waterfall also inspired William Cullen Bryant’s poem Catterskill Falls.

moments.title: Palenville
moments.text: Kaaterskill Creek runs through Palenville at the foot of the clove. The hamlet takes its name from the Palen family, whose Catskill tanneries depended on hemlock bark. When the local bark supply ran out, the tannery closed. Tourism followed, with boardinghouses and a claim to be the home of the fictional Rip Van Winkle. Thomas Cole and Frederic Church stayed and worked here during the Hudson River School’s height. At the turn of the century, nearly two dozen boardinghouses and many hotels served vacationers here. The creek’s swinging footbridge was destroyed during Tropical Storm Irene.
